  • a fixed address
  • proof of legitimate income
  • no criminal record
  • a mental health test
  • proof you know how to handle a gun and shoot it

I started out my medical career as a mental health tech and became a RN. I worked as a psych nurse for a couple of years and in hospitals for 30 years. I have done thousands of intake interviews and taken many psycho social histories. Anyone like me would only need about a 10 minute conversation with someone to figure out whether or not we would want to be around them if they were armed. It is not as subjective as you think. If you are around crazy people much their mental problems will be clearly apparent.

May I ask what your life dangers are that you feel the need for a gun? In my 63 years of life I have had one coworker who was present during a armed robbery of a fast food restaurant, one relative who committed suicide with a gun and one drunk relative who killed another armed drunk in a skuffle. I have cared for perhaps a hundred people with gunshot wounds. Most of those people were shot by relatives, other gang members, themselves. In many of the cases involving altercations with neighbors and casual contacts most seemed, by the stories they told me, to have been avoidable. Being around drunks and getting involved in pissing contests were not helped by having one of the parties armed.

I don't want to be misconstrued in any way. My supplied reasoning was based to some extent on the realities in Brazil itself, and to some extent my personal views as a US citizen. The difference between what Brazil is proposing/currently has, and what we have here in the US is at the crux of my objection to the "mental health" rules. In Brazil, the criteria for a "failed" mental heath examination could be deliberately complex, contradictory or convoluted by design, to disenfranchise as many individuals as possible. Ownership of a firearm is a currently a privilege, like owning a new cellphone, or a car. It's very easy to put arbitrary limitations on privileges, as it's easier to set conditions when you're giving something to someone, as opposed to when you're trying to take away something they already have.

In the US, owning a firearm is a constitutional right. Taking that away from people requires a much more solid legal framework, not an opinion (which, educated or otherwise are subjective) based on a 10 minute conversation. Many mental illnesses, unlike physical diseases, do not have readily identifiable, objectively apparent symptoms. Can you prove, legally that someone "hears voices" telling them to do something bad? Or that someone has "recovered" from violent impulses beyond their control? Sure, you can test, medically for things like chemical imbalances, physical abnormalities with the brain, etc. But on it's best day, a psychological evaluation of an individual is at most an opinion about someones mental state based on a short conversation. As an example, I point to the rules and laws regarding involuntary commitment. To just temporarily relieve someone of one of their rights (freedom, in this case) requires a rather strict set of conditions, all setup so that the individual can challenge and require verifiable proof that they pose a danger. With that in mind, how many people whom you feel shouldn't own a gun would meet the criteria for involuntary commitment, and how many would "stick" (i.e. not have the commitment dismissed legally)?

As for my personally, I don't feel the need to carry a firearm most of my life. I didn't buy any because I felt I needed to ward off danger, I own them because I enjoy the sporting aspects (3 gun, marksmanship, IDPA). I'm of the mindset that if you go looking for trouble, you'll often find it.

As a personal anecdote, I have friends that work in a variety of fields in which they DO carry a weapon daily. One is a store owner in a rather bad area. He's been robbed 3 times in the last decade. The first time he spent a week in the hospital with a fractured skull. He was lucky, and learned his lesson after the first time and openly carries at work now. The last two robberies, he held the would-be robber at bay until police arrived. Many people (myself included) live in a rural setting. The reality is If I call the police at 3AM (which I have had to do. Someone breaking into my car), it'll be 10 minutes or so before anyone can show up (the guy ended up getting away long before the police arrived). Say that individual wanted what was in my house, instead of my car. Should I be required to subject myself to whatever a tweaked out home invader (something that's happening at a growing rate in my area due to drug addicts seeking funds) has in mind for my family while I wait around for law enforcement?

In the US right now, conservatively 30% of the US population owns something like 300 million firearms. When it comes to Violent crime involving a gun, only 3% of them are committed with a legally owned weapon. If just owning a firearm was the problem, there would be a staggeringly different statistic there. Criminals obviously don't care about regulations.

Various simulators and some 3rd and 1st person RPGs mostly. From what I've read it's supposed to be great for 3rd person games but not so sure about 1st person? As for 3rd person; how would it work for something like Pillars of Eternity (if you've played that)? Does it take a lot of practice to be as efficient as one would be with a mouse and keyboard?

Have you tried it with racing games or anything involving operating a vehicle? I usually prefer an XBox controller for that, as I like having analog controls for steering and throttle but can't be arsed with a bulky wheel+pedals setup that I need to assemble and disassemble every time I want to go for a drive.

I've played a few fps games with the steam pad, and it does require some getting used to. Most importantly you need to setup the gyro controls, which allow you to look around by moving the controller (it is great for precise aiming). I definitely feel like I have more speed and precision as compared to a regular joystick controller, but it isn't quite as good as a keyboard.

Haven't played PoE, but that seems like a perfect fit for the steam controller. The controller is easily reprogrammable through steam big picture, so you can set your bindings as you like, or use one of the community created key mappings. 3rd person games are probably the easiest fit for this controller, it should be really easy to pick it up in these cases.

Also haven't tried racing games, but it seems like it would be a good fit there as well. Pressure sensitive keys to allow for graduated accel/decel, potential to use the accelerometer.
